excerpt: Paano magtanim ng bawang? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant bawang (garlic), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

heroImage.alt: Onion plants in beds separated by grassy paths on a Philippine farm

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant bawang. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

How Ilocano and other Filipino farmers grow native garlic in rice fields right after the harvest, without plowing, under a cover of rice straw. The small native bulbs are strong in flavor and keep for months when cured well.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for onion and garlic](/land-preparation/onion-garlic-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [bawang varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/garlic). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [bawang nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/garlic-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing.
When to plant bawang

Planted from October to November in the Ilocos Region and other lowlands, right after the rice harvest, and pulled about four months later. Planting in December or later usually gives smaller bulbs. Garlic is also grown this way in Mindoro and in a few highland areas in the cool months.
What you plant

Cloves from bulbs kept from the last harvest and hung to dry. Bulbs are broken into cloves only a day or two before planting, and farmers use the big, firm outer cloves and throw out small, soft or damaged ones. Some soak the cloves in water overnight before planting.
Paano magtanim ng bawang, step by step
The crop is ready about 120 days after sowing.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 3 days before sowing: Cut the stubble
items.text: Right after the rice harvest, cut the rice stubble and any weeds down to ground level. The field is not plowed. If the soil is too dry, let water in briefly and drain it so the soil is moist but firm.

items.title: 1 day before sowing: Prepare the cloves
items.text: Break the bulbs into cloves and sort out the big, firm ones. Soak them in water overnight if you follow that habit.

parts.title: Take down the seed bulbs
parts.text: Take down the bundles of big, firm bulbs that were set aside and kept hanging since the last harvest. Pass over bulbs that are soft, moldy or already shriveled.

parts.title: Break them just before planting
parts.text: Separate the cloves only a day or two before planting, by pressing the bulb apart with the thumbs. Cloves broken apart too early dry out and come up weak.

parts.title: Sort the cloves
parts.text: Keep the big, firm outer cloves with their skins on. Set aside the small inner cloves for the kitchen and throw out any that are soft, bruised or moldy.

parts.title: Soak them if that is your habit
parts.text: Some farmers soak the sorted cloves in clean water overnight and plant them the next morning, so they root quickly in the moist soil.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Sowing day: Fertilizer before planting
items.text: Many farmers spread complete fertilizer (14 14 14) over the field before planting.

items.title: Sowing day: Push the cloves in
items.text: Push each clove, pointed end up, about 2 to 3 cm into the soft soil, about 15 x 15 cm or 20 x 10 cm apart. A string or a marked stick keeps the rows straight.

items.title: Sowing day: Cover with rice straw
items.text: Cover the whole field with a layer of rice straw about 3 to 5 cm deep. It keeps the soil moist and smothers most weeds.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 2: First watering
items.text: Let water flow into the field from a canal or a pump until the soil is wet, then drain it off quickly. Repeat about every week or two in the dry months, depending on the soil.

items.title: Day 30: Side dress
items.text: Scatter urea (46 0 0) or ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) over the mulch and water it in. Some farmers add potash (0 0 60) later as the bulbs form.

items.title: Day 30: Pull the weeds
items.text: Hand pull the weeds that come through the straw.

items.title: Day 40: Watch the leaves
items.text: Check for thrips (silvery streaks), purple blotch and leaf tip burn, which spread in humid weather, and for caterpillars on the leaves.

items.title: Day 100: Stop watering
items.text: Stop watering about two to three weeks before harvest so the bulbs mature firm.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Day 120: Pull when the leaves yellow
items.text: Harvest when most leaves have turned yellow or brown and the stems start to bend, about four months after planting. Pull the plants by hand.

items.title: Day 121: Dry in the field
items.text: Lay the plants in rows with the leaves covering the bulbs and leave them to dry for a few days.

items.title: Day 125: Bundle and hang
items.text: Tie the plants in bundles by their leaves and hang them under the house or in an airy shed to cure. Garlic is kept this way until it is sold or planted.

parts.title: Tie bundles by the leaves
parts.text: Once the leaves have dried in the field, gather the plants in handfuls and tie them in bundles by their leaves, bulbs hanging down.

parts.title: Hang them in an airy shade
parts.text: Hang the bundles on poles under the house or in a shed where air moves freely, out of the sun and the rain. Garlic keeps best in a warm, dry place, not a damp one.

parts.title: Keep the best for planting
parts.text: Set aside bundles of the biggest, firmest bulbs from the healthiest plants as next season's seed. They stay hanging until planting time.

parts.title: Guard the stored bulbs
parts.text: Look the bundles over now and then and take out bulbs that rot or sprout. Some Ilocos farmers dry the bulbs on a cement floor before storing and lay dried lagundi leaves among them to keep off the small beetles that bore into stored garlic.
parts.time: 7 to 10 days on the cement floor

parts.title: Trim when you sell
parts.text: When the garlic goes to market, cut off the roots and the dry leaves, leaving a short neck on each bulb.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for bawang
Spacing
About 15 x 15 cm, or 20 x 10 cm, cloves pushed 2 to 3 cm deep.
Water
Watered by letting water from a canal or a pump flow over the field and draining it off quickly, about every week or two in the dry months, then stopped two to three weeks before harvest.
Fertilizer

Complete fertilizer (14 14 14) spread before planting, then urea (46 0 0) or ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) at about a month, sometimes with potash (0 0 60) as the bulbs form. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-vegetables-philippines).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows
The thick rice straw mulch does most of the weeding, and the rest is hand pulled. Farmers watch for thrips and leaf diseases, which are worse in humid weather.
When and how to harvest
Ready about four months after planting, when most leaves have yellowed. Plants are pulled, dried in the field for a few days, then tied in bundles and hung in the shade to cure.
Common mistakes when planting bawang

items: Planting late, in December or after, which gives small bulbs.
Planting small, soft or damaged cloves.
Leaving water standing in the field, which rots the cloves.
Watering up to harvest, so bulbs are soft and store poorly.
Harvesting too early, so the bulbs shrink as they dry.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of bawang
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Plant only big, healthy cloves, ideally from a clean field without disease.
Plant on time, in October to November, right after the rice harvest.
Test the soil and match the fertilizer to it.
Keep the straw mulch even, 3 to 5 cm thick, and never let water stand.
Cure the bulbs well in the shade before storing or selling.
